name: Lehali
confidence_why: No source describes Lehali word stress itself: François 2005 says only that essentially all Torres-Banks languages, Lehali among them, now stress the final syllable, and Codrington 1885, Tryon 1976, Lynch and Crowley 2001, François 2011 and the 2021 Pangloss archive say nothing about stress, so any placement is an areal inference rather than an observation.

catalog_quote: [p.451] In the case of northern Vanuatu languages, there is every likelihood that the final consonants of POc forms had been lost at some stage (e.g., ‘ten’ *saŋapuluq > *saŋapulu); this resulted in vowel-final lexemes that systematically received primary stress on their penultimate syllable, and secondary stress every second syllable leftward (e.g., *saŋapulu). Vowel reduction affected word-medial as well as word-final posttonic syllables,9 which explains why words with four syllables were regularly reduced to two: for example, *saŋapulu > MSN saŋwul. The loss of word-final posttonic vowels explains why, in essentially all the languages of the area, words are now systematically stressed on their final rather than their penultimate syllable (contra Lynch 2000:77). ... [fn.2 p.443] The data cited in the present paper were collected by the author during three field surveys: ... July–August 2004 for Mota, Lehali, Lo-Toga, and Hiu. ... [p.469] Interestingly, although Dorig is otherwise a well-behaved oxytone language (e.g., [marmar] ‘hard’), the presence of a long /a/ word-internally tends to attract word stress: [rar]. ... [Guy 1978 PL C-61 p.782] Word-stress does not seem to have existed in PNNH as it appears to have been innovated along different rules in Sakao, Lehali, and Shark Bay.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File checked: (symlink to, author's open copy of François 2005, Oceanic Linguistics 44(2):443-504). The quoted passage is at sec. 3.1 'Prosodic stress and vowel reduction', p.451 (the text; re-extracted independently with extracted text and matched). Wording is identical; the only differences are that the quote drops the footnote callout '9' after 'posttonic syllables' and normalises the PDF font glyphs (the text shows *sa¥apulu / '²nal' for *saŋapulu / 'final'; the printed stress diacritics on *saŋapulu do not survive extraction). Key sentence confirmed: 'The loss of word-final posttonic vowels explains why, in essentially all the languages of the area, words are now systematically stresse…
new_statements.rule_in_words: In the modern Torres-Banks languages (Lehali being one of the 17 surveyed on the author's own data), primary word stress falls on the final syllable, the historical result of losing all post-tonic vowels after a penultimate-stress stage.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Only historical: proto-forms had secondary stress every second syllable leftward of the penult; nothing stated about synchronic secondary stress in Lehali.
new_statements.exceptions: Hedged as 'essentially all the languages of the area' (Mota retained many final vowels and is the implicit outlier); no Lehali-specific exception given; Lehali is listed (Table 12) as having lost all posttonic vowels, so it falls squarely under the generalization.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level ('words are now systematically stressed on their final.. syllable'); areal/comparative statement, not a dedicated synchronic description of Lehali; François 2007 adds that the article proclitic n- lacks its own stress in all Torres-Banks languages.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement is areal: François 2005 covers 17 Torres-Banks languages, with Lehali (LHI, tql, leha1243) included on the author's own 2004 fieldwork; it is not a sentence about Lehali alone. No dedicated grammar/phonology of Lehali exists (Glottolog descriptive refs = 0; Lynch & Crowley 2001: no phonology). Codrington 1885's 'Retan' (western Ureparapara) dialect in his Norbarbar sketch matches the Lehali sound profile (r > y, b > p) but has no accent note; his 'Alo Teqel' is a Vanua Lava dialect despite Glottolog's alt name 'Teqel' for Lehali. Distinct from Löyöp/Lehalurup (leha1244) on east Ureparapara.

readall_conflicts: Lynch 2000 (pp.59, 77) treats Mwotlap, Lehali's Banks neighbour, as a regular penultimate-syllable-stress language on the basis of Crowley's second-hand TOL sketch; François 2005:451 (the existing statement, first-hand data on all 17 Torres-Banks languages including Lehali) states 'contra Lynch 2000:77' that words in essentially all languages of the area are now systematically stressed on their final rather than their penultimate syllable, because the posttonic final vowels were lost. The disagreement concerns Mwotlap, not Lehali directly; for Lehali, Lynch 2000 says nothing, so the only statement on the record remains François 2005's areal final-stress statement, which was written specifically to correct the Lynch passage. No source opened gives a Lehali-specific stress rule.

sources.note: Sec. 3.1 p.451: proto-forms had penultimate primary stress + secondary stress every second syllable leftward; loss of final posttonic vowels means 'in essentially all the languages of the area, words are now systematically stressed on their final rather than their penultimate syllable (contra Lynch 2000:77)'. Areal statement covering Lehali; Table 12: Lehali lost all posttonic vowels; p.467 ex.(29) Lehali 4-syllable etyma (historical stress asymmetry). No Lehali-specific synchronic stress sentence.
